builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: The Noise Floor of a Quantization Comparison: Engine, restart, batch and kernel drift, measured against 8-bit and 4-bit effects in two decision models
summary: This methodology replaces aggregate accuracy comparison by measuring decision-level changes against a baseline noise floor encompassing engine restarts, batching variations, and kernel selection differences. It requires recording per-sample outputs across multiple inference runs and engine configurations, adding engineering overhead to the evaluation pipeline. Reliance on aggregate metrics can fail to detect substantial per-decision regressions—such as 436 degraded decisions offset by improvements elsewhere—leading to deployment of models that appear stable but alter behavior on individual inputs.
rationale: Adopting per-record evaluation against measured noise floors is essential when deploying quantized models on constrained infrastructure, as aggregate accuracy metrics conceal significant decision-level instability that can determine production viability.
technique: Quantization-aware benchmarking with noise floor measurement

claims.statement: This methodology replaces aggregate accuracy comparison by measuring decision-level changes against a baseline noise floor encompassing engine restarts, batching variations, and kernel selection differences. It requires recording per-sample outputs across multiple inference runs and engine configurations, adding engineering overhead to the evaluation pipeline. Reliance on aggregate metrics can fail to detect substantial per-decision regressions—such as 436 degraded decisions offset by improvements elsewhere—leading to deployment of models that appear stable but alter behavior on individual inputs.

4-bit quantization exceeds all non-quantization noise sources (0–0.92% decision flips), with Q4_K_M altering 5.79% of decisions on Clef-flash versus 0.88% at Q8_0; accuracy aggregates mask these changes, showing net differences as small as -0.02 points despite 436 individual decision regressions.
